title: Setup
text:
Please complete the following steps before the workshop so we can dive straight into the material.
You’ll need:

A recent version of Positron.
Signed up for posit.ai using the same email address as your course registration. Open Posit Assistant in Positron and connect your posit.ai account. (It’s fine to use other tools but there are a couple of things we want to show you specifically in PA.)
Grab the development version of PA by pressing Cmd + Shift + P to open the command palette and paste Posit Assistant: Check for newer dev build. Follow the prompts to restart your current PA.
Install pak with install.packages("pak") and then ensure you have the latest devtools and associated packages with pak::pak("devtools").

title: Best practices feedback loop
text:
LLMs amplify best practices, and make them more achievable
Virtuous cycle: where as you improve tests and docs, it makes it easier for agents to work with your package.
Really good news for non-professional developers
You can do as you go, but also useful to batch up as part of regular upkeep

title: Best practices feedback loop
text:
Just use air

No longer worth manually enforcing a coding style
Just use air
Get started with usethis::use_air() + Air: format workspace file.
(If you’re using the Claude Code extension, it won’t know where to find the air binary. You can tell that it’s bundled in )

title: Best practices feedback loop
text:
Beware excessive comments

Agents (esp. Claude) LOVE to write wordy comments
Sometimes the comments are useful; often they are not
Code-comment mismatch more dangerous with agents
Comments should explain the why
Comments shouldn’t need to explain the what
Comments shouldn’t explain how we got here
I’ve had relatively little success prompting this behaviour away
Better luck with prompt to remove

title: Best practices feedback loop
text:
Agents love to write tests

Generally don’t need to explicitly ask for them
(Assuming you have tests already set up e.g. with use_testthat())
Explicitly request code coverage
May want to explicitly request TDD (i.e. write the test first)

title: Best practices feedback loop
text:
Your job is to:

Keep them well organised

“Tests for R/{foo}.R should live in tests/testhat/test-{foo}.R”

Keep them fast

“Parallelise these tests”
“Use SlowReporter and speed up the slowest tests”
“Compare coverage before and after”

Keep them minimal

“Carefully consider the tests”

All these tasks are faciliated by relatively fine grained R and test files
You can ask the agent to refactor

title: Best practices feedback loop
text:
Test coverage

Previously 100% test coverage was not worth it.
Probably worth reconsidering now.

title: Best practices feedback loop
text:
Test maintenance

Worth asking to minimise tests, to group related tests together
Make sure

title: Best practices feedback loop
text:
Overview

LLMs are very good at improving the performance of code.
They are better than me at reading the results of RProf().
They are better than me at writing C/C++ code.
They are not very good at experimental design.
They are not very good at managing complexity/performance tradeoffs.

title: Best practices feedback loop
text:
Prompting

“Make XXX faster”
Make sure it’s well tested first
Ensure it records its work
Request both microbenchmarks and meaningful user actions
Pay attention to what it’s doing

title: Best practices feedback loop
text:
C/C++

Previously C++ (via Rcpp/cpp11) had good balance of effort vs. results
Now for small amounts of compiled code, pure C has no dependencies and LLMs are good at writing it.
You will need to give it hints as to latest C API.

title: How do agents work?
section: Life is good for individual developers
text:
Life is good for individual developers

Individuals can use an all-you-can-eat plan

Codex: $20 / month, $100 / month
Claude Code: $20 / month, $100 / month

These are very generous; you get 20-80x what the API costs
BUT you can only use in provider harnesses
(So you can’t use claude code subscription with PA :sad-face:)

title: How do agents work?
text:
Enterprise plans are different

Enterprises have to pay by the million tokens

Opus 5: $5 input, $25 output
gpt-5.6-terra: $2 input, $12 output
Kimi K3: $3 input, $15 output

(This is also what you pay in ellmer)

title: How do agents work?
text:
Why care?

At least in the short-term this is really important for organisations, and I think data scientists and engineers need to understand where they’re spending money.
Two tools:

Posit Assistant
AgentsView

In both cases these are best-efforts to compute cost. Model providers don’t make this easy!
Skills (which we’ll come back to later are a good way to increase token efficiency)

title: How do agents work?
section: My views on cost-benefit have changed
text:
My views on cost-benefit have changed

I used to think that Anthropic was worth the additional cost.
But the relative cost has increased and output quality has decreased (code is still fine, but the sheer quantity of AI slop writing is painful)
Kimi K3 is excellent. Somewhere between Opus and Fable in quality. But much more concive. And only costs 75% of sonnet (thanks to tokenizer).

title: How do agents work?
text:
Tokenizers

By and large, you don’t need to care about the details of going from text to the numbers that LLMs us
BUT in [TODO: fill in model] Claude switched to a tokenizer that produces ~30% more tokens for the same input.
So in general, there are lots of other levers providers can pull.
And you might wonder if Claude’s loquacious output is a way to raise prices.
Assessing total cost is hard :(

title: How do agents work?
section: Cost is dominated by cache hits
text:
Cost is dominated by cache hits

No caching = ~10x cost
Of course it would be very slow if each time the conversation had to restart from scratch
So providers cache the results of the previous turn so that they can resume where they left off
Caching price still iterating, but seems to be stabilising

You pay more to cache results: 1.25x
Cache reads are much cheaper: 0.1x
The conversation records explicit cache points

Details for cache length vary:

Claude: 5 minutes / 1 hour (2x cost)
OpenAI: 30 minutes
KimiK3: no guarantees

Very difficult to figure out the exact consequences of costs.
But if you step away from a claude session for 5 minutes, the next request might be 10x the cost. We’re working on better tools for this in PA.

title: How do agents work?
text:
Compaction is no longer relevant

In past generations of models, with smaller context, harness would provide tools for compaction
Basically, you ask a model (maybe the same as existing maybe) to summarise
The problem is you lose the advantages of caching

title: How do agents work?
section: Agents can run code on your computer
text:
Agents can run code on your computer

Send tool call request; harness runs and sends results
Often does many of these in parallel (in a single turn, not at the same time )
The LLM sends a bunch of requests, your harness does them sequentially, then sends a bunch of responses

title: Modern R Workflow (ft. Positron and AI)
text:
Instructors

Hadley Wickham
Hadley Wickham is Chief Scientist at Posit, where (among other things) he leads the tidyverse team. He builds tools (both computational and cognitive) that make data science easier, faster, and more fun. He’s the creator of packages like ggplot2, dplyr, and devtools and an author of several books on R, including R for Data Science and R Packages.
GitHub · Bluesky · LinkedIn


Jenny Bryan
Jenny Bryan is a Senior Software Engineer at Posit, where she works on the tidyverse/r-lib and Positron teams. A recovering biostatistician, she takes special delight in eliminating the small agonies of data analysis. She’s the creator of packages like googlesheets4 and reprex and an author of the book R Packages and the Happy Git with R guide.
GitHub · Bluesky

title: Modern R Workflow (ft. Positron and AI)
text:
Description
This workshop is designed for data scientists who are comfortable with using R for data analysis and ready to level up their software engineering skills. Led by Hadley Wickham and Jenny Bryan, you’ll learn how to write more robust, maintainable R code while taking advantage of modern tooling (cough AI cough) that can dramatically accelerate your productivity.
We’ll cover three interconnected themes. First, you’ll learn contemporary R development practices—writing functions, organizing code into packages, testing, and documentation strategies that scale from personal projects to team collaboration. Second, we’ll explore how AI assistants like Claude Code can help you write better R code faster. Third, we’ll share practical tips for getting the most out of Positron, including features specifically designed to make R development and data exploration more fluid.
Throughout the workshop, we’ll emphasize the connections between these topics: how good development practices make AI assistance more effective, how modern tooling reduces friction so you can focus on the interesting problems, and how to build workflows that are both efficient and reproducible. You’ll leave with concrete skills you can apply immediately to your own projects.
Prerequisites: Basic familiarity with R programming (e.g., using the tidyverse). You should have written a few functions before, but don’t need any experience with package development, AI coding tools, or Positron. If you have taken a package development workshop before, you’ll learn what’s changed in our workflows, especially how we’re using AI and Positron effectively.
